messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Children Present: Being around children, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo was twenty-four when the assault occurred during a family reunion. He had stepped into the unheated laundry room of his relative’s house to wait for a glass of water. The specific temperature on his forearms, the exact chill of the tile seeping through his dress shoes, remains seared into his recall. The door clicked shut behind him. He does not remember the encounter as something completed years ago; the memory arrives unbidden during morning routines or while he is reviewing files, forcing its way into his mind with such clarity that his skin still tenses when a draft catches his wrists. He carries a heavy sense of contamination, certain that the dirt of what happened can never be fully washed away. Alongside this, he holds the conviction that his body has been permanently damaged. These realities sit with him, unbroken by time, occupying the same mental space without intersecting. As a prosecutor, Mateo’s professional environment became the stage where his daily patterns took root. He developed a steady habit of avoiding unfamiliar courtrooms and municipal offices, telling himself he could not assess the danger in unknown spaces. At the same time, scanning for exits became automatic; he mapped the nearest route out the moment he crossed any threshold. His attention naturally fixed on potential weapons: the heavy letter openers on conference tables, the glass display cases in the clerk’s lobby, the metal fire extinguishers mounted near the loading docks. These behaviors did not replace one another; they ran together, layering over his routine. When the building’s HVAC system dropped the temperature, that precise sensation on his skin would arise independently, and he would abruptly leave meetings under the pretense of an urgent deadline. The accumulation of these experiences reshaped his personal life. He stopped attending family gatherings because the presence of related people brought the old violation forward with undeniable force. His two adult children live only two hours away, but he no longer visits their homes. Being around their young grandchildren brings a sharp awareness of physical vulnerability, while the warmth of their house’s radiators mirrors the exact temperature that precedes his distress. He does not link these sensations to one another; they simply arise side by side, making the household feel impossible to navigate. His wife’s passing five years ago left the house quiet, and he has carried the isolation alone, reading newspapers for reports of violence and walking through his neighborhood with his shoulders permanently tightened, certain that the world is a dangerous place. Now at sixty-seven, Mateo sits in the quiet of his study, surrounded by case files he has stopped accepting. The uncontrolled access of the memories has begun to fracture his sleep, and the parallel weight of contamination and vulnerability has grown too heavy to bear alone. He walked into the clinic last Tuesday because he could no longer navigate his days without counting doors or waiting for the temperature to shift. He is afraid that speaking about the past will seal the contamination permanently, that the danger he expects will finally arrive. Yet, beneath the fear, he hopes someone can help him find a way to sit in a room without the memories forcing their way forward, so he might finally rest.
